title: The Woman Who Watered Stone
summary: For forty years, old Marda has watered a bare grey stone in her garden every single day, waiting for it to bloom. The village calls her mad. But when young Tomas comes to learn from her, he discovers the truth is stranger and wiser than madness — and learns the hard difference between faithful patience and stubborn folly.

chapters.title: The Stone in the Garden
chapters.body:
In the village of Stillwater, everyone knew about mad old Marda and the stone she watered.

For as long as anyone could remember — forty years, the old folk said — Marda had gone out into her garden every single morning, rain or shine, winter or summer, and watered a stone. Not a plant. A stone. A bare, grey, ordinary stone, about the size of a loaf of bread, sitting in the middle of an otherwise beautiful and thriving garden. Every morning, without fail, she filled her watering can and poured water carefully over the grey stone, as if it were a seed she expected to bloom. And every morning, the stone did exactly what stones do, which is nothing. It sat there, grey and bare and stony, year after year after year.

The village found this by turns funny, sad, and unsettling. Children dared each other to sneak into Marda's garden and look at the famous watered stone. Grown-ups shook their heads and murmured that the old woman had lost her wits, watering a rock for forty years, waiting for a stone to flower. Some pitied her. Some mocked her. All of them agreed she was mad — kindly mad, harmlessly mad, but mad — because who but a madwoman would water a stone every day for forty years, expecting it to bloom?

Tomas was fifteen, and he was a serious, curious boy, and he did not like easy answers. And the easy answer about Marda — that she was simply mad — did not satisfy him. Because he had watched the old woman, and she did not seem mad in any other way. She was sharp, and wise, and kind, and clear-eyed about everything else in her life. She ran her thriving garden with great skill. She gave good advice to those who asked. She was, in every respect but the stone, one of the most sensible people in Stillwater. And Tomas thought: a person that wise, doing a thing that strange, for that long — perhaps there is something here that isn't madness at all. Perhaps there is something to understand.

So Tomas went to old Marda, and asked if he might learn from her — not just about gardening, but about the stone. And Marda looked at him with her sharp clear eyes, and something in them warmed, as if she had been waiting a long time for someone to ask instead of mock.

"Most people just laugh," she said. "Or pity me. You're the first in a long while to think there might be something worth asking about." She handed him a watering can. "Come, then. Water the stone with me, every morning, and watch, and we'll see what you learn. But I'll warn you — what you learn may not be what you expect. It never is."

chapters.title: Faithful or Foolish
chapters.body:
So Tomas watered the stone with Marda every morning, and watched, and waited to understand. And for a long time, he learned nothing but that watering a stone is exactly as pointless as it sounds. The stone did nothing. It sat there, grey and bare, drinking water that ran off its sides into the earth, and never changed at all.

And Tomas began to wrestle with the question that the whole village had already answered too easily. Was Marda faithful, or was she foolish? Because there were two ways to see what she did, and they looked almost identical from outside, and Tomas could not tell which was true.

On the one hand, perhaps Marda was faithful — patient in some deep, wise way the village couldn't see. Perhaps she knew something about the stone that others didn't. Perhaps her forty years of watering were not madness but a profound and beautiful patience, a faith that would someday be rewarded, the kind of steady devotion that the hasty mocking world had simply lost the capacity to understand.

But on the other hand — and Tomas made himself consider this honestly — perhaps Marda was simply foolish. Perhaps she was doing a pointless thing, and had done it so long she couldn't stop, and dressed up her stubbornness as patience because she couldn't bear to admit forty years had been wasted. Perhaps "faith" was just the pretty word she used for an inability to let go of something that was never going to work. And this troubled Tomas deeply, because he had seen that kind of thing too — people who kept doing a hopeless thing, and called it faith or patience or persistence, when really it was just stubbornness, or fear of admitting they'd been wrong.

He asked Marda about it directly, one morning, because he was that kind of boy. "How do you know," he said, "that you're being patient, and not just stubborn? How do you know watering the stone is faith, and not foolishness? They look the same from here. Everyone says you're mad. How do you know they're wrong?"

And Marda, instead of being offended, smiled — a deep, pleased smile, as if Tomas had finally asked the right question.

"That," she said, "is the question. That's the whole question. And most people never ask it — not about me, and not about themselves. They can't tell the difference between faithful patience and stubborn folly, because from outside, and even from inside, they look exactly the same. A person watering a stone that will bloom, and a person watering a stone that never will, are doing the identical thing. The difference isn't in the watering. It's in something else." She poured her water over the grey stone. "Let me ask you something, boy. You've assumed, like everyone, that I water this stone because I expect it to bloom. That I'm waiting for a flower. What if that's not why I water it at all?"

Tomas was startled. "Then... why would you water a stone, if not to make it bloom?"

"Ah," said Marda. "Now you're closer. Keep watering. Keep watching. And soon I'll tell you the truth of it — which is neither the faith the kind ones imagine, nor the folly the cruel ones assume, but a third thing, that only the ones who bother to ask ever learn."

chapters.title: What the Watering Was For
chapters.body:
Finally, after Tomas had watered the stone with her for a full turning of the seasons, old Marda sat him down in her thriving garden and told him the truth.

"I do not water this stone because I think it will bloom," she said. "I knew, forty years ago, on the first morning, that it was a stone, and that stones do not bloom. I have never once expected a flower. So you see, I am not the fool the village thinks — I'm not waiting for something impossible, deceiving myself year after year. I've known the truth about the stone from the very beginning."

Tomas was baffled. "Then why? Why water a stone for forty years, if you never thought it would bloom? What's it for?"

Marda gestured around her — at the garden, the most beautiful and thriving garden in all of Stillwater, bursting with life and color and abundance. "Look at my garden, Tomas. Really look at it. In forty years, have you ever seen one more alive?"

Tomas looked, and had to admit he hadn't. Marda's garden was extraordinary — richer, greener, more full of life than any other in the village.

"Every morning for forty years," Marda said, "I have gone out to water the stone. And to reach the stone, in the middle of my garden, I walk through all of it. And watering the stone every single day, without fail, in rain and shine and winter and summer, has made me a person who goes out into her garden every single day, without fail, and looks at everything, and tends everything, and never once neglects it. The stone is not why my garden thrives. But watering the stone is. The discipline of it. The daily faithful practice of it. The stone gave me a reason to show up, every single day, no matter what — and a person who shows up every single day, and walks through her whole garden, and pays attention, cannot help but tend it well. The stone never bloomed. But everything around the stone bloomed, because of the stone."

And Tomas began, at last, to understand.

"You asked me," Marda went on, "how to tell faithful patience from stubborn folly, when they look the same from outside. Here is the answer, and it's the deepest thing I know. The difference is not whether the thing you're faithful to comes true. It's whether the faithfulness itself makes you and the world around you better, whether or not it comes true. A stubborn fool waters a dead thing hoping it will live, gets nothing, and is diminished — bitter, deceived, wasted. But a wise one is faithful to a practice because the practice itself bears fruit, all around it, whether or not the thing at its center ever changes. I was never really watering the stone, Tomas. I was using the stone to make myself faithful — and the faithfulness watered everything else. That's not folly. And it's not even quite the blind faith the kind ones imagine. It's something wiser than both: choosing a devotion not for what it promises to give you, but for who it makes you as you practice it."

Tomas sat with this for a long time, and felt it settle into him as one of the truest things he'd ever heard. He'd thought the question was whether the stone would bloom — whether Marda's faith would be rewarded, whether her patience would pay off. But that had been the wrong question all along. The stone would never bloom; Marda had always known that; and it didn't matter. Because the watering — the daily, faithful, disciplined showing-up — had already borne fruit, forty years of it, in the most beautiful garden in the village and in the wise, steady, present person Marda had become by practicing it. The faithfulness had been its own reward, and had watered everything around it, precisely because it was never really about the stone.

"The village thinks I'm mad," Marda said, "because they think I'm waiting for a stone to bloom. But I've never been waiting for anything. I've been practicing something. And the practice made my garden, and made me, and that was always the point. When you go looking for something to be faithful to in your own life, Tomas, don't choose it for what it promises to give you — a stone promises nothing, and gives everything. Choose a practice, a devotion, a daily faithful showing-up, that makes you better and waters everything around it as you do it. Then it doesn't matter whether the thing at the center ever blooms. You'll have bloomed. And so will everything you tended along the way."

Tomas grew up to be a wise man himself, and he was known all his life for a deep and steady faithfulness — a way of showing up, every day, to the things and people he'd chosen to tend, without fail, in rain and shine. And when people asked him how he'd learned such patience, such devotion, he told them about old Marda and the stone she watered for forty years. He told them she was not mad, and not even simply faithful in the way people imagined, but something wiser: a woman who understood that the point of a faithful practice is not whether the thing at its center ever changes, but who you become, and what blooms around you, as you faithfully tend it. "She watered a stone every day for forty years," he would say, "and the stone never bloomed, and it didn't matter at all — because she bloomed, and her garden bloomed, and everyone who learned from her bloomed. That is the difference between faithful patience and stubborn folly. The fool is faithful to a thing for what it will give him, and is diminished when it gives nothing. The wise one is faithful to a practice for who it makes her — and everything around her flowers, whether or not the stone ever does."
